structure.title: 4. Inference using fixed length confidence intervals

observations.statement: The target is stated as a linear combination of post-treatment causal effects (a single period effect or the average across post periods), defined within a generic event-study coefficient vector that is decomposed into causal effects and a differential trend.

Rather than exact parallel trends, identification comes from a researcher-specified set of admissible differential trends that links post-treatment violations to the identified pre-trends; the usual parallel trends assumption is nested as a special case. Partial identification of the target is derived under this set.

The paper motivates its approach by listing concerns with current practice: pre-trends tests can be underpowered, conditioning on passing them distorts inference, and parametric trend controls are sensitive to functional form.

Several named restriction classes are defined (relative magnitudes, smoothness or second differences, their combination, sign and monotonicity, general polyhedral), each linked to an intuitive argument applied researchers commonly make about confounders.

No-anticipation is stated explicitly as the assumption that makes pre-period causal effects zero, for both non-staggered and staggered DiD examples; the ATT is chosen as target with a footnote on how ATE bounds could be obtained.

The framework is explicitly linked to staggered-adoption estimators (Callaway and Sant'Anna style aggregates), IV event studies and covariate-adjusted DiD, with the interpretation of the bias term restated for each variant.

The inferential goal is stated as uniform coverage over the identified set and over the restriction class, first in a finite-sample normal model with known variance and then translated into uniform asymptotic size control with an estimated covariance matrix.

The regularity conditions are justified by noting that event-study coefficients are usually OLS with cluster-robust variance estimators, which are asymptotically normal as the number of clusters grows; joint normality of estimate and variance estimate is assumed without independence.
The first-stage size of the least-favourable hybrid test is fixed at a fraction of the nominal level, and the choice is attributed to prior work rather than tuned to the data.
observations.quote: we use κ = α/10, following ARP

observations.statement: The recommended inference procedure depends on the restriction class: the hybrid moment-inequality confidence set for generic polyhedral classes, and fixed-length confidence intervals only where consistency and finite-sample near-optimality are guaranteed (smoothness class).

For the first application, the event-study coefficients are plotted and a joint test of the pre-period coefficients is reported as a formal pre-trends test, with the visual pattern of pre versus post coefficients described alongside it.
For the second application, event-study coefficients are plotted separately by gender and the visual shape of the pre-period coefficients is used to motivate the smoothness restriction class.

For both applications, the reported robust confidence sets are compared with the sample analogue of the identified set in the supplementary appendix, to separate the roles of sampling uncertainty and identified-set length.
observations.locator: Section 6.2 and 6.3, references to Supplementary Appendix C

observations.statement: The main empirical output is a sensitivity plot: robust confidence sets for the target parameter traced over a grid of the restriction parameter, with the original OLS confidence interval shown as a benchmark and the breakdown value for a null effect identified.

In the first application, results are shown for two estimands (a single post period and the average across post periods), and the paper explains why the identified set widens for later periods under consecutive-period bounds.

Simulation results on size control, an alternative target parameter, additional restriction parameters, and simulations drawn from the empirical distribution of the original data rather than the normal model are delegated to the supplementary material.

Simulations are calibrated to the estimated event-study covariance matrices of recently published papers surveyed in a prior study, using each paper's own clustering scheme; coefficients are drawn from a normal model around a chosen mean vector.
The empirical illustrations reuse published replication packages of two prior papers, cited with their repository DOIs in the reference list; one dataset is acknowledged as shared by an author.
observations.locator: Section 6.2, 6.3; Acknowledgments; References (Benzarti and Carloni 2019a, Lovenheim and Willen 2019b)

observations.statement: For each application the unit and data source are restated from the original paper: firm-year panel with a control group of other market-service firms; state-by-birth-cohort-by-survey-year cell averages from the American Community Survey.

Outcome and treatment definitions of the reused specifications are restated: log before-tax profits with a restaurant indicator interacted with year dummies; cohort-level employment with event-time indicators relative to the year a cohort turned eighteen, with endpoints binned.

The authors change the omitted event-time period from the original paper's choice to an earlier period because the original reference period may be partially treated, which would violate the assumption of no pre-period causal effect.
observations.quote: we instead treat event-time −2 as the reference period

observations.statement: In simulations, the restriction parameter and pulse magnitude are expressed in units of the standard error of the first post-period coefficient so that results are comparable across the calibrating papers and interpretable as worst-case bias relative to standard error.

Reused regression specifications are written out as equations with fixed effects and controls named in the text, and the cluster level of the original standard errors is stated for the first application.
The paper reports no regression tables; the only table summarizes which theoretical properties hold for each simulation design, and all empirical and simulation results are conveyed by figures.

Event-study coefficient plots are shown for each application before the sensitivity analysis, and sensitivity results are presented as confidence-set plots against the restriction parameter with the original OLS interval in a distinct colour.

Simulation performance is shown as curves of a median efficiency ratio across calibrating papers against a normalized restriction or pre-trend parameter, with figure notes stating the number of simulations per paper, colours per procedure and the definition of the ratio.
A schematic figure is used to illustrate when a constraint qualification holds or fails, with the note spelling out each panel's configuration.
No significance stars are used; conclusions are phrased in terms of whether confidence sets exclude zero at a given restriction parameter and where the breakdown value lies.

The smoothness parameter is given an economic scale by a calibration exercise that maps a change in slope of the differential trend into an equivalent shift in teacher value-added using an estimate from prior literature.

The breakdown value of the relative-magnitudes parameter is interpreted against context (a recession in the first post year) to discuss whether post-period confounding shocks could plausibly exceed the pre-period maximum by that factor.
Robust confidence sets are compared in width with the original OLS interval and with the estimated identified set, and the paper reports how long the sensitivity computations take on a named laptop.

A footnote notes that treatment timing in the second application is staggered so the original two-way fixed effects coefficients have a causal interpretation only under homogeneous effects; the authors keep the original specification for simplicity and note that heterogeneity-robust estimators could be used instead.

The optimal local power result is qualified: its asymptotics assume sampling variation is small relative to the identified set, so it may not approximate finite-sample performance under point identification or short identified sets.

The paper states that it targets inference on the causal parameter given a restriction, not inference on the breakdown point or frontier, while noting in a footnote a one-sided interval for the breakdown point and leaving uniform frontier coverage to future work.

Fixed-length confidence intervals are shown to be inconsistent for restriction classes built from pre-period maxima or sign and shape restrictions, and the paper warns against using them outside the smoothness class.

In the second application the analysis is run separately for men and women, following the original paper, and the discussion contrasts how the same smoothness restriction changes conclusions across the two groups.

The introduction previews the framework, both inference approaches, the theoretical power results, the simulation-based recommendation and the two applications before a separate related-literature subsection.
The paper is ordered as model set-up, two inference sections, a simulation study, then a practical-guidance section that precedes the empirical illustrations, and a short conclusion.
A three-period non-staggered DiD running example is continued through the model section to illustrate each restriction class and the identified set.

A dedicated practical-guidance subsection instructs applied researchers on choosing the restriction class from domain knowledge, choosing the inference procedure and reporting sensitivity and breakdown values.
Proofs, additional simulation results, an alternative benchmark bound and the identified-set comparisons are all placed in supplementary material, referenced by appendix letter.
Some formal results are not reproduced; the text refers readers to specific propositions in the working-paper version of the same paper.
A data availability statement gives a Zenodo DOI for the data and code underlying the paper.
The methods are implemented in named R and Stata packages whose GitHub URLs are given in footnotes, and a package co-developer is credited in the acknowledgments.
Application data are taken from public replication archives of the original papers hosted at the AEA data repository, cited by DOI.
A footnote states that the framework applies to any asymptotically normal reduced-form estimator satisfying the causal decomposition, such as first differences or triple differences.

Simulation performance is benchmarked against an optimal expected-length bound for valid confidence sets, with a sharp bound for convex classes and a possibly non-sharp bound for unions of convex sets, stated in a footnote.
The simulation section states that size control was found to be good for all procedures and therefore focuses the main text on power comparisons, moving size results to the supplement.
